This study presents a novel calibration method for high-precision stellar photometry, designed to achieve measurement accuracy sufficient for determining the vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) with precision comparable to satellite instruments. The primary challenge lies in the fact that the photometric calibration curve is non-linear and exhibits significant variability, particularly at the faint magnitudes typically observed in VAOD studies. To address this, we developed a new calibration approach that integrates a non-linear model with a random walk prior to account for short-term fluctuations. We applied this method to approximately 100 nights of data collected by a 10 cm telescope at the University of Chile. The results indicate that the new approach yields a 20% reduction in calibration uncertainty relative to the standard technique. Furthermore, the resulting photometric measurements align more closely with those from the AERONET satellite network, demonstrating that this method enables the determination of VAOD with the required precision for satellite-level accuracy. The detailed procedures and findings of this work are available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00300.

This method relies on high-precision stellar photometry, which demands extreme observational accuracy. We detail the implementation of this approach using a low-cost, small-aperture telescope and a commercial-grade camera. Our analysis of roughly 100 nights of data from a 10 cm telescope at the University of Chile demonstrates that this technique is feasible with modest equipment. The results show that the new method reduces calibration uncertainty by 20% compared to the conventional approach, bringing VAOD precision closer to that of satellite instruments. Additionally, the calibrated photometric measurements exhibit greater consistency with ground-based satellite observations from AERONET. We introduce a novel definition of operator complexity applicable to conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, grounded in the expectation value of the squared commutator between the vacuum and a unitarily evolved state. Utilizing the holographic duality between quantum field theory and gravity, we derive a universal lower bound for this complexity that aligns with the well-known causal wedge bound. We demonstrate that this upper bound adheres to a characteristic logarithmic-square growth pattern. Finally, we provide explicit calculations of both the lower and upper bounds for specific models, including the free massless scalar field and the free Lax pair within the context of Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton-axion gravity. These findings suggest that the universal coefficient governing the growth of complexity lies between the derived lower and upper limits. Our results indicate that, for both the free scalar field and the Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton-axion model, the lower bound serves as a reliable approximation of the actual complexity. Additionally, for the latter model, we observe that the universal coefficient in the gravitational dual closely matches the value predicted by the complexified geodesic method. Ultimately, we propose a refined lower bound for the squared commutator-based complexity in 1+1 dimensional conformal field theories, which corresponds to the complexified causal wedge in the holographic dual. This new bound is strictly tighter than the conventional causal wedge limit. As a byproduct, we also derive an explicit formula for the complexity within the Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton-axion model. Our analysis confirms that, for this specific model, the complexity defined by the complexified geodesic and the complexified causal wedge remains identical. This study examines the bilepton model, which extends the Standard Model's gauge symmetry to $SU(3)_C\times SU(2)_L\times U(1)_R\times U(1)_B$. The analysis covers the model's renormalization, the generation of fermion masses and mixing, the implementation of symmetry breaking, and the identification of new physics phenomena. It is demonstrated that, under specific conditions, the model's symmetry breaking mechanism aligns with that of the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM). Furthermore, the existence of bileptons is shown to offer a viable solution to the muon $g-2$ anomaly. The research also investigates the potential for bileptons to generate neutrino masses via the seesaw mechanism and for the lightest supersymmetric particle to serve as dark matter. Finally, the study outlines the decay channels of heavier supersymmetric particles and baryons, providing a comprehensive overview of the model's phenomenology. The implications of adopting a modified gauge group are detailed, with particular attention given to the potential for baryon number violation. Ultimately, the work concludes that the bilepton model represents a viable extension of the Standard Model, capable of addressing multiple unresolved issues. Additionally, the model's phenomenological features are compared with those of other models featuring an enlarged gauge group. The findings presented here complement and expand upon the research detailed in reference [1]. By incorporating a bilepton, the bilepton model introduces a new particle with spin-1 and non-zero baryon and lepton numbers, carrying the quantum numbers $B=\pm 2$ and $\Delta L=\pm 2$. This particle can mediate the transition between two baryons, altering their lepton number by two units. Consequently, the stability of the proton is no longer guaranteed, as baryon number violation becomes possible. Nevertheless, the model's viability relies on the bilepton being sufficiently massive to suppress this violation to levels consistent with current experimental constraints. To satisfy these limits, the mass of the lightest bilepton must exceed approximately 1.5 TeV. Achieving such a high mass scale requires specific conditions regarding the fermion sector, which are elaborated upon in the following sections. Additionally, the model must account for the observed neutrino masses and mixing angles. While the seesaw mechanism is a common approach to generating small neutrino masses, it is not the only option. In this work, we explore an alternative method for generating neutrino masses within the bilepton framework.

Bipartite graphs are frequently illustrated using two parallel lines of vertices, with edges represented as straight segments connecting them. A primary goal in these visualizations is to reduce edge crossings, yet achieving this often results in drawings that are stretched or distorted. This paper introduces a novel metric for crossings that permits curved edges, enabling a significant decrease in crossings without compromising aesthetic quality. We demonstrate that minimizing this new metric is NP-hard and provide both hierarchical and non-hierarchical approximation algorithms. Furthermore, we introduce a linear-time 2-approximation algorithm for the non-hierarchical approach. Our proposed metric and corresponding algorithms are applicable to any point-set graph, including those with non-bipartite structures. To validate our methods, we analyzed a collection of 1,000 real-world bipartite graphs, comparing our results against state-of-the-art techniques. The outcomes indicate that our new metric yields drawings with fewer crossings and superior aesthetics. Additionally, we offer an implementation of our algorithms available at https://github.com/GraphXie/BiCross. Our analysis of real-world datasets reveals previously unknown structures and patterns, highlighting the potential of this metric to uncover hidden insights in large-scale data. Ultimately, we argue that adopting a new definition of crossings can enhance the aesthetic quality of graph drawings and facilitate the discovery of previously unidentified structures in real-world datasets. These findings indicate that workload degradation methods can be significantly strengthened by exploiting SMT features. Additionally, we present a comprehensive analysis of the factors influencing the success of these techniques, offering practical guidance for selecting optimal configurations. Finally, we validate the practical utility of CPA-T by enabling the extraction of secret keys from AES and ChaCha20 implementations, achieving performance comparable to full side-channel attack frameworks. The student network then learns from the teacher's refined weights alongside the questions and answers. To address the challenge of limited labeled data, the study employs a semi-supervised learning framework. The authors hypothesize that the student network will benefit from the teacher's knowledge graph, which is derived from a small set of labeled questions and answers combined with an extensive knowledge graph. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in both supervised and semi-supervised settings. Furthermore, the semi-supervised performance of the Teacher-Student architecture surpasses that of a single network. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/KG-Student.

Furthermore, we introduce a novel variant of the test designed for scenarios where data points are missing at random. Finally, we provide Python code to facilitate the execution of this new variant. To address this, we propose a modified version that achieves robust performance across diverse metric types and data distributions. This study introduces a new metric, the Diachronic Contextualized Embedding Distance (Diced), designed to identify diachronic semantic change (DSC) through contextualized embeddings. We introduce a novel method for determining the mass and spin of black holes in Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) by utilizing their electromagnetic spectra. These features manifest as breaks or flattening in the power spectrum of variability. By fitting a physical model to the variability spectrum, we can infer the central black hole's mass and spin. This technique is applicable to AGN exhibiting strong variability, provided the variability amplitude exceeds 0.15 over timescales shorter than 20 days. We demonstrate the method's validity using the variable star RS Puppis and the AGN NGC 4051. Furthermore, we apply this method to a sample of 100 nearby AGN to infer their black hole masses, finding that the resulting mass distribution aligns well with expectations. This new methodology offers an independent means to measure black hole masses, complementing existing methods and potentially resolving discrepancies in the inferred mass distribution of local black hole X-ray binaries. Ultimately, this approach could help identify intermediate mass black holes within the local universe. Our analysis code is accessible at https://github.com/aharvard/AGNQNMs. The significance of this work lies in the development of a new technique to infer black hole masses in AGN, which serves as an independent verification of current methods and may uncover intermediate mass black holes in the local universe. Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) represents a minimally invasive technique for ablating brain tissue, offering a viable alternative to surgical resection for recurrent gliomas. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of LITT in reducing tumor volume and enhancing neurological function in patients with recurrent high-grade gliomas who were not candidates for further surgical removal. The analysis included 12 patients who underwent LITT at a single center between 2011 and 2015. Tumor ablation was confirmed via MRI, and the extent of ablation was categorized into three groups: less than 50%, between 50% and 75%, and greater than 75%. Post-procedural MRI scans were assessed to identify complications, while neurological function was monitored using the Karnofsky Performance Scale (KPS) and the Rankin Scale. The median duration of ablation was 20 minutes, with a mean total procedure time of 100 minutes. Complications occurred in 33% of cases, primarily manifesting as transient seizures or transient neurological deficits. The median tumor volume reduction was 60% (interquartile range: 30-80%), with 58% of patients achieving a reduction of at least 50%. At the six-month follow-up, the median KPS score increased from 60 to 70, and 83% of patients demonstrated an improvement in their Rankin score. These findings indicate that LITT is a safe and effective method for reducing tumor volume and potentially improving neurological function in patients with recurrent high-grade gliomas who cannot undergo additional surgical resection. Future research should focus on optimizing ablation volumes and determining the most suitable patient selection criteria. The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01390600).

The results align closely with those obtained via standard state reconstruction techniques. This method offers a practical and efficient way to monitor non-Gaussian states of light. Additionally, we present a simplified procedure for deriving the Woerner-Hudson-Charney (WHC) representation directly from the optical slice probability distribution. Finally, we apply this technique to generate the WHC representation for a Schrödinger cat state. Our findings indicate that the optical slice probability distribution contains sufficient information to fully reconstruct the state within the harmonic oscillator framework. Ultimately, this study provides a practical framework for directly extracting the Wigner function and WHC representation from the optical slice probability distribution, enabling the effective monitoring of non-Gaussian states of light.

Backdoor attacks represent a significant threat in machine learning, where an adversary embeds a hidden trigger into a model during training. Upon deployment, the model behaves normally until the trigger activates, causing it to output a pre-determined target. While numerous methods have been developed to detect and mitigate these attacks, they often incur substantial computational costs or fail to address sophisticated attack variants. Instead, our approach leverages a lightweight neural network to analyze the output distributions of a potentially compromised model. By employing a distribution-based strategy, we effectively detect various backdoor techniques, including those with complex triggers, image-specific triggers, and even state-of-the-art methods like PolyGlot and BImp. Extensive evaluations across multiple datasets and attack scenarios demonstrate that our method achieves high detection accuracy while maintaining low computational overhead. Furthermore, we show that this framework can be adapted to detect backdoor attacks in other deep learning architectures. Extensive simulations using both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that Balanced Sampling significantly outperforms existing non-IID mitigation strategies. We introduce a novel multiplexing configuration for lobster-eye (LE) optics, designed to enhance the effective area of wide-field X-ray monitors. This approach involves segmenting the LE optic into multiple smaller units, each paired with a dedicated detector, and integrating them into a single system. We evaluated this multiplexed setup using a 100 cm focal length LE optic and a 10x10 cm focal plane, comparing its performance against a conventional single-unit design. Our analysis covered the point spread function (PSF), effective area, and source localization precision. Results indicate that the multiplexed configuration achieves an effective area nearly 2.5 times greater than the single unit, while maintaining comparable PSF and localization accuracy. This design offers a viable solution for scaling up the focal plane of LE-based X-ray monitors without compromising imaging quality. Furthermore, it presents a practical method for deploying large-area LE optics, which are otherwise difficult to manufacture. The potential benefits of this approach are particularly significant for future X-ray monitors with focal planes exceeding 1 meter in size. Additionally, this study provides a framework for optimizing the segmentation of multiplexed LE optics to maximize effective area while preserving imaging fidelity. The Meissner effect, which causes a superconductor to expel its internal magnetic field, is a defining characteristic of superconductivity. This phenomenon enables the levitation of a superconductor above a magnet, as illustrated in the accompanying image. While the expulsion of the field is evident, the underlying mechanism remains a subject of ongoing debate. This paper presents a detailed analysis of the interaction between a thin, flat, two-dimensional (2D) superconducting disk and an external magnetic field. We demonstrate that the expulsion of the field from the disk's interior is driven by the diamagnetic Meissner current flowing within the material. Furthermore, we show that the magnetic field lines are not expelled from the surrounding space but are instead redirected around the disk. By modeling the field lines as elastic strings, we derive the shape of these lines in the area surrounding the disk. Additionally, we examine the behavior of the field lines within the disk itself, revealing that they follow a helical trajectory. Finally, we calculate the force acting on the disk and determine the conditions under which levitation occurs. Our findings indicate that the expulsion of the magnetic field from the surrounding space is not required for the disk to levitate. Instead, levitation results from the interaction between the diamagnetic Meissner current and the local magnetic field, a mechanism analogous to the Lorentz force. This interaction generates a repulsive force that counteracts gravity, enabling levitation even when the magnetic field lines penetrate the disk. Our results suggest that the expulsion of the field from the surrounding region is merely a consequence of the interaction between the Meissner current and the local field, rather than the direct cause of levitation. Consequently, the expulsion of the magnetic field from the surrounding space is unnecessary for the levitation of a 2D superconducting disk. Our calculations also provide a method for estimating the critical current density required for levitation. These conclusions are derived using the Ginzburg-Landau theory, which remains valid for the specific parameters of the system under study. This paper introduces a deep learning approach designed to detect skin cancer from images, serving as an entry for the ISIC challenge 2019. The primary objective is to classify image data into one of five categories: melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, actinic keratosis, dermatofibroma, and benign nevi. To achieve this, we propose a novel architecture called the Multi-Stage Attention Network (MSAN), which integrates a multi-stage framework with attention mechanisms. The model processes input through three sequential stages: a convolutional neural network (CNN) for feature extraction, a global average pooling layer, and a fully connected layer. In the second stage, the extracted features are divided into two groups, each fed into a distinct attention mechanism. Finally, the outputs from both attention mechanisms are combined and passed through a fully connected layer to generate the final classification. The network was trained and evaluated using the public ISIC 2018 dataset, which comprises 10,000 labeled images. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed MSAN architecture outperforms other methods on this dataset, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.893 and an accuracy of 0.901. These findings confirm the effectiveness of the proposed architecture for the skin cancer detection task. Furthermore, the model was tested on the external ISIC 2017 dataset, yielding a macro F1 score of 0.889 and an accuracy of 0.896, indicating strong performance on unseen data. The source code for this work is available at: https://github.com/AbdulWahab1997/MSAN.
